claim: Insulin signaling controls metabolic homeostasis.
source: Insulin signaling controls metabolic homeostasis.
evidence: This is a general statement about insulin signaling function, representing established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of full-length insulin receptor (IR) and insulin complex in the active state was determined.
source: Here, we report the cryo-EM structure of full-length insulin receptor (IR) and insulin complex in the active state.
evidence: The manuscript reports the determination of this structure as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Maximally four insulins can bind the 'T'-shaped IR dimer at four distinct sites related by 2-fold symmetry.
source: This structure unexpectedly reveals that maximally four insulins can bind the 'T'-shaped IR dimer at four distinct sites related by 2-fold symmetry.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM structure reported in the manuscript.

claim: Insulins 1 and 1' bind to sites 1 and 1', formed by L1 of one IR protomer and α-CT and FnIII-1 of the other.
source: Insulins 1 and 1' bind to sites 1 and 1', formed by L1 of one IR protomer and α-CT and FnIII-1 of the other.
evidence: This describes the structural observation of insulin binding sites from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Insulins 2 and 2' bind to sites 2 and 2' on FnIII-1 of each protomer.
source: Insulins 2 and 2' bind to sites 2 and 2' on FnIII-1 of each protomer.
evidence: This describes the structural observation of insulin binding sites from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Both sites 1 and 2 are required for optimal insulin binding and IR activation.
source: Mutagenesis and cellular assays show that both sites 1 and 2 are required for optimal insulin binding and IR activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis and cellular assays described in the manuscript.

claim: A homotypic FnIII-2–FnIII-2 interaction mediates the dimerization of membrane proximal domains in the active IR dimer.
source: We further identify a homotypic FnIII-2–FnIII-2 interaction in mediating the dimerization of membrane proximal domains in the active IR dimer.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Binding of multiple insulins at two distinct types of sites disrupts the autoinhibited apo-IR dimer and stabilizes the active dimer.
source: Our results indicate that binding of multiple insulins at two distinct types of sites disrupts the autoinhibited apo-IR dimer and stabilizes the active dimer.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on structural and functional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: IR is a receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) that plays essential roles in glucose metabolism and cell growth.
source: Insulin receptor (IR) is a receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) that plays essential roles in glucose metabolism and cell growth (Ullrich et al., 1985).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Dysregulation of IR signaling is linked to many human diseases, such as diabetes and cancers.
source: Dysregulation of IR signaling is linked to many human diseases, such as diabetes and cancers (Olefsky, 1976).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: IR forms a stable homodimer covalently linked by multiple disulfide bonds.
source: Unlike most RTKs, IR forms a stable homodimer covalently linked by multiple disulfide bonds (Schäffer and Ljungqvist, 1992; Sparrow et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IR has two distinct insulin-binding sites with different affinities for insulin, termed sites 1 and 2.
source: Previous mutagenesis and binding studies have suggested that IR has two distinct insulin-binding sites with different affinities for insulin, termed sites 1 and 2 (De Meyts, 1994).
evidence: This is prior knowledge from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: A single insulin molecule simultaneously engages site 1 of one IR protomer and site 2 of the other, thus bridging the two IR protomers.
source: It has been further proposed that a single insulin molecule simultaneously engages site 1 of one IR promtomer and site 2 of the other, thus bridging the two IR protomers (De Meyts, 1994; Schäffer, 1994).
evidence: This is a prior model from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The crystal structure of the extracellular domain of IR in the absence of insulin reveals an inverted 'V' shaped architecture.
source: The crystal structure of the extracellular domain of IR (comprising L1, CR, L2, FnIII-1,–2,−3 domains) in the absence of insulin was solved first (McKern et al., 2006), revealing an inverted 'V' shaped architecture.
evidence: This is prior structural knowledge from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: The crystal structure of the IR extracellular domain bound to insulin shows that one insulin molecule binds to the primary site, which consists of the L1 domain and the C-terminal helix of the α chain (α-CT).
source: The crystal structure of the IR extracellular domain bound to insulin was subsequently determined (Menting et al., 2013), showing that one insulin molecule binds to the primary site, which consists of the L1 domain and the C-terminal helix of the α chain (α-CT).
evidence: This is prior structural knowledge from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: Insulin binding induces a large conformational change in IR and converts the overall architecture of IR dimer from an autoinhibited inverted 'V' shape to a 'T' shape.
source: Recently, three groups, using single-particle electron microscopy (EM), showed that insulin binding induces a large conformational change in IR (Gutmann et al., 2018; Scapin et al., 2018; Weis et al., 2018) and converts the overall architecture of IR dimer from an autoinhibited inverted 'V' shape to a 'T' shape.
evidence: This is prior knowledge from recent literature, supported by citations.

claim: The conversion to 'T' shape brings the two kinase domains of the IR dimer into close proximity to enable efficient trans-autophosphorylation and activation.
source: This conversion has been proposed to bring the two kinase domains of the IR dimer into close proximity to enable efficient trans-autophosphorylation and activation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on prior structural studies.

claim: A new IR–insulin interface involving a loop of FnIII-1 has been proposed to represent site 2 of IR.
source: Two of the three studies (Gutmann et al., 2018; Weis et al., 2018) also identified a new IR–insulin interface involving a loop of FnIII-1. This interface has been proposed to represent site 2 of IR.
evidence: This is prior knowledge from recent literature, supported by citations.

claim: The overall resolution of the full-length human IR–insulin complex structure is 3.2 Å.
source: Here, we report the cryo-EM structure of the full-length human IR–insulin complex at an overall resolution of 3.2 Å.
evidence: This is a direct report of the resolution achieved in the cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: Sites 1 and 1' are formed by the L1 domain of one IR protomer and α-CT and the FnIII-1 loop of the other.
source: Sites 1 and 1' are formed by the L1 domain of one IR protomer and α-CT and the FnIII-1 loop of the other.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Sites 2 and 2' are located on the back of a main β sheet of the FnIII-1 domain of each protomer.
source: Sites 2 and 2' are located on the back of a main β sheet of the FnIII-1 domain of each protomer.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Mutagenesis, binding and cellular assays confirm the new IR–insulin interface as the authentic site 2.
source: Our mutagenesis, binding and cellular assays, along with insulin mutations in the previous literature (De Meyts, 2015; Kristensen et al., 1997), confirm this new IR–insulin interface as the authentic site 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the current study and prior literature.

claim: The results revise and extend the widely accepted 'crosslinking' model of IR activation.
source: Therefore, our results revise and extend the widely accepted 'crosslinking' model of IR activation, and indicate that binding of multiple insulin molecules to two distinct types of sites on each IR dimer breaks the auto-inhibited state and fully activates IR.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural and functional data in the context of prior models.

claim: The D1120N mutation inactivates IR kinase activity.
source: To improve the expression yield, we introduced several mutations in the intracellular domain of IR, including the D1120N mutation that inactivates its kinase activity and the Y960F mutation that has been shown to reduce clathrin-mediated endocytosis of IR (White et al., 1988; Choi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a functional characterization of a mutation used in the study.

claim: The Y960F mutation reduces clathrin-mediated endocytosis of IR.
source: To improve the expression yield, we introduced several mutations in the intracellular domain of IR, including the D1120N mutation that inactivates its kinase activity and the Y960F mutation that has been shown to reduce clathrin-mediated endocytosis of IR (White et al., 1988; Choi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is prior knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Recombinant IR isolated with detergent binds insulin with high affinity and displays strong negative cooperativity (Hill coefficients of ~0.62).
source: Recombinant IR isolated with detergent binds insulin with high affinity and displays strong negative cooperativity (Hill coefficients of ~0.62), comparable to our and other's cell-based insulin-binding results (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D) (De Meyts et al., 1973).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from in vitro binding assays.

claim: All resolved 3D reconstructions exhibited almost perfect 2-fold symmetry.
source: During cryo-EM image processing, initial 3D classification was produced without any symmetry imposed. All the resolved 3D reconstructions, however, exhibited almost perfect 2-fold symmetry (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that insulins bind to the majority of IR in a symmetrical manner.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM image processing.

claim: Insulins bind to the majority of IR in a symmetrical manner.
source: All the resolved 3D reconstructions, however, exhibited almost perfect 2-fold symmetry (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that insulins bind to the majority of IR in a symmetrical manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed 2-fold symmetry in the 3D reconstructions.

claim: The resolution for the top part of the complex was improved to 3.1 Å after focused refinement.
source: To further improve the resolution, we performed a focused refinement (as described in our previous work, Wong et al., 2014) for the top part of the IR–insulin complex, including the L1, CR, L2, and FnIII-1 domains of IR as well as all the bound insulins. As a result, the resolution for the top part of the complex was improved to 3.1 Å (Figure 1B), allowing us to build a nearly complete atomic model for this region (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 4).
evidence: This is a report of the resolution achieved after focused refinement.

claim: The cryo-EM densities for the FnIII-2 and FnIII-3 domains were less well resolved, presumably due to structural flexibility.
source: The cryo-EM densities for the FnIII-2 and FnIII-3 domains were less well resolved, presumably due to structural flexibility.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data with a speculative explanation.

claim: The densities of kinase domains were completely unresolved in the cryo-EM map.
source: The densities of kinase domains were completely unresolved in the cryo-EM map.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The IR dimer exists in an extended 'T'-shaped arrangement with 2-fold symmetry in the full-length IR–insulin complex.
source: In the full-length IR–insulin complex, the IR dimer exists in an extended 'T'-shaped arrangement with 2-fold symmetry (Figure 1), in agreement with the 2D class averages of full-length IR in the presence of insulin obtained previously by negative-stain EM (Gutmann et al., 2018) as well as the recently solved cryo-EM structure of the IR extracellular domain bound to insulin (Scapin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure, consistent with prior studies.

claim: The horizontal part of the 'T' is composed of the L1, CR and L2 domains of both IR promoters.
source: The horizontal part of the 'T' is composed of the L1, CR and L2 domains of both IR promoters.
evidence: This is a structural description from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The vertical piece of the 'T' consists exclusively of the FnIII-1, FnIII-2 and FnIII-3 domains of the IR dimer.
source: The vertical piece of the 'T' consists exclusively of the FnIII-1, FnIII-2 and FnIII-3 domains of the IR dimer.
evidence: This is a structural description from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The two FnIII-3 domains are separated by ~120 Å in the apo-form of the IR dimer.
source: The apo-form of the IR dimer exhibits an inverted 'V' shape, with the two FnIII-3 domains separated by ~120 Å (McKern et al., 2006).
evidence: This is prior structural knowledge from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: The two kinase domains are likely separated by a long distance in the autoinhibited conformation and cannot undergo efficient trans-autophosphorylation.
source: Because the FnIII-3 domain is connected to the transmembrane (TM) domain and intracellular kinase domains through a short linker (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), the two kinase domains are likely separated by a long distance and cannot undergo efficient trans-autophosphorylation in this autoinhibited conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural arrangement in the apo-form.

claim: The distance between the two FnIII-3 domains in the 'T'-shaped insulin-bound IR dimer is reduced to ~40 Å.
source: The distance between the two FnIII-3 domains in the 'T'-shaped insulin-bound IR dimer, however, is reduced to ~40 Å.
evidence: This is a structural measurement from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The two TM domains may dimerize in the IR–insulin complex.
source: In addition, the partially resolved density for the single-pass TM domain suggests that the two TM domains may dimerize in the IR–insulin complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on partially resolved density.

claim: The two intracellular kinase domains are expected to be in close proximity in the 'T'-shaped conformation, enabling their trans-autophosphorylation.
source: The two intracellular kinase domains are thus expected to be in close proximity in this 'T'-shaped conformation, enabling their trans-autophosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural arrangement in the active form.

claim: The 'T'-shaped conformation of the IR dimer represents an active form.
source: Therefore, this conformation of the IR dimer represents an active form.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural features that enable kinase activation.

claim: Four insulins are bound to four sites in the fully liganded IR dimer.
source: Strikingly, we can identify four insulins bound to four sites in the fully liganded IR dimer (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Insulin 1 at site 1 buries 706 Å2 of solvent-exposed surface areas of IR.
source: Insulin 1 at site 1 and insulin 2 at site 2 bury 706 and 394 Å2 of solvent-exposed surface areas of IR, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structural analysis.

claim: Insulin 2 at site 2 buries 394 Å2 of solvent-exposed surface areas of IR.
source: Insulin 1 at site 1 and insulin 2 at site 2 bury 706 and 394 Å2 of solvent-exposed surface areas of IR, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structural analysis.

claim: Site 1 likely has higher affinity in insulin binding than site 2.
source: Thus, site 1 likely has higher affinity in insulin binding than site 2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the buried surface area measurements.

claim: 63% of the particles have four insulins bound (two each at sites 1 and 2).
source: In particular, 63% of the particles have four insulins bound (two each at sites 1 and 2), while 33% of the particles have three insulins bound (two at site 1; one at site 2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from focused classification analysis.

claim: 33% of the particles have three insulins bound (two at site 1; one at site 2).
source: In particular, 63% of the particles have four insulins bound (two each at sites 1 and 2), while 33% of the particles have three insulins bound (two at site 1; one at site 2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from focused classification analysis.

claim: There is only a subtle difference between the structures of IR with three or four insulins bound.
source: There is only a subtle difference between the structures of IR with three or four insulins bound, which indicates that binding of insulins to both sites 2 and 2' is not required for the maintenance of the T-shaped IR dimer (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from structural comparison.

claim: Binding of insulins to both sites 2 and 2' is not required for the maintenance of the T-shaped IR dimer.
source: There is only a subtle difference between the structures of IR with three or four insulins bound, which indicates that binding of insulins to both sites 2 and 2' is not required for the maintenance of the T-shaped IR dimer (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison.

claim: 96% of the T-shaped particles have at least one insulin bound to site 2 or 2'.
source: Importantly, the vast majority (96%) of the T-shaped particles have at least one insulin bound to site 2 or 2', suggesting that insulin binding to site 2 is important for IR to adopt the active T shape.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from focused classification analysis.

claim: Insulin binding to site 2 is important for IR to adopt the active T shape.
source: Importantly, the vast majority (96%) of the T-shaped particles have at least one insulin bound to site 2 or 2', suggesting that insulin binding to site 2 is important for IR to adopt the active T shape.
evidence: This is an inference based on the particle distribution analysis.

claim: Another study deposited in the preprint server bioRxiv showed a low-resolution cryo-EM map of the IR extracellular domain with four insulins bound at sites 1 and 2.
source: During the revision of this manuscript, another study deposited in the preprint server bioRxiv also showed a low-resolution cryo-EM map of the IR extracellular domain with four insulins bound at sites 1 and 2 (Gutmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a reference to concurrent work by another group.

claim: The 3:1 or 4:1 stoichiometry of insulin binding to the IR dimer is consistent with previous IR–insulin binding assays that indicated the coexistence of high- and low-affinity insulin-binding sites.
source: The 3:1 or 4:1 stoichiometry of insulin binding to the IR dimer and the two types of binding sites are consistent with previous IR–insulin binding assays that indicated the coexistence of high- and low-affinity insulin-binding sites (Schäffer, 1994).
evidence: This is a comparison of current findings with prior literature.

claim: Previous results were interpreted with a binding equilibrium of 2:1 stoichiometry, and may need to be reexamined in light of the current findings.
source: Those results were, however, interpreted with a binding equilibrium of 2:1 stoichiometry, and in light of our findings here may need to be reexamined.
evidence: This is a suggestion for reinterpretation of prior data based on new findings.

claim: Insulin 1 binds mainly through the primary site formed by the L1 domain and α-CT.
source: Insulin 1 binds mainly through the primary site formed by the L1 domain and α-CT (Figure 2A, left panel).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: IR is an intertwined domain-swapped homodimer.
source: Nevertheless, based on previous biochemical and structural results (Chan et al., 2007), IR is an intertwined domain-swapped homodimer.
evidence: This is prior knowledge from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: The two elements that constitute the primary site, the L1 domain and α-CT, are from two different IR protomers.
source: Thus, the two elements that constitute this primary site, the L1 domain and α-CT, are from two different IR protomers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the domain-swapped structure of IR.

claim: The primary insulin–IR interface is nearly identical to that observed in the crystal structure of the IR extracellular domain bound to insulin.
source: This primary insulin–IR interface is nearly identical to that observed in the crystal structure of the IR extracellular domain bound to insulin (Menting et al., 2013), and will not be described in detail.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior structural data.

claim: IR R14E and F714A mutants exhibited deficient insulin-dependent IR activation.
source: To confirm that insulin binding to this site is essential for IR activation, we introduced R14E (Whittaker and Whittaker, 2005) and F714A mutations into IR to disrupt this interface, and showed that both IR R14E and F714A mutants, when expressed in human 293 cells, exhibited deficient insulin-dependent IR activation (Figure 2B, and 2C).
evidence: This is an experimental result from cellular assays.

claim: Insulin 1 makes contact with a loop of the FnIII-1 domain from the IR protomer that has donated α-CT.
source: In addition to this primary interface, insulin 1 makes contact with a loop of the FnIII-1 domain from the IR protomer that has donated α-CT (Figure 2A, left panel).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The secondary interface at site 1b was first observed in a previously reported cryo-EM study of the IR extracellular domain bound to insulin.
source: This secondary interface was first observed in the previously reported cryo-EM study of the IR extracellular domain bound to insulin (Scapin et al., 2018), but could not be accurately modeled due to the low-resolution density map and had been erroneously assigned as site 2.
evidence: This is a reference to prior work with a correction of its interpretation.

claim: At site 1b, two disulfide-bonded cysteines (Cys A7 and Cys B7) and His B5 of insulin pack against Pro495, Phe497, and Arg498 in the IR FnIII-1 domain through hydrophobic interactions.
source: At site 1b, two disulfide-bonded cysteines (Cys A7 and Cys B7) and His B5 of insulin pack against Pro495, Phe497, and Arg498 in the IR FnIII-1 domain through hydrophobic interactions (Figure 2A, left panel).
evidence: This is a detailed structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Insulin binding induces the formation of a new interface between the FnIII-1 domain and α-CT of the same protomer.
source: In addition, insulin binding induces the formation of a new interface between the FnIII-1 domain and α-CT of the same protomer (Figure 2A, left panel), which only exists in the 'T'-shaped active dimer.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The interface between FnIII-1 and α-CT involves a cluster of charged residues, including Asp496, Arg498 and Asp499 in the FnIII-1 domain and Lys703, Glu706 and Asp707 in α-CT, which form multiple salt bridges.
source: This interface involves a cluster of charged residues, including Asp496, Arg498 and Asp499 in the FnIII-1 domain and Lys703, Glu706 and Asp707 in α-CT, which form multiple salt bridges (Figure 2A, left panel).
evidence: This is a detailed structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: An IR D707A mutation has been found in patients with leprechaunism, a rare genetic disease with severe insulin signaling defects.
source: Notably, an IR D707A mutation has been found in patients with leprechaunism, a rare genetic disease with severe insulin signaling defects (Hart et al., 1996).
evidence: This is prior clinical knowledge from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: The D707A mutation may affect IR activation by disrupting the interface between FnIII-1 and α-CT.
source: This mutation may affect IR activation by disrupting this interface.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural observation.

claim: The F497A mutant showed markedly reduced insulin-dependent IR activation.
source: To test the functional relevance of site 1b, we mutated the residue Phe497 of IR (which contacts insulin) to alanine, and tested its effect on IR activation. The F497A mutant showed markedly reduced insulin-dependent IR activation (Figure 2B, and 2C).
evidence: This is an experimental result from cellular assays.

claim: The D496A, R498E, D707A, and K703A mutants all showed greatly reduced activation.
source: We next introduced several point mutations (D496A, R498E, K703A, and D707A) into IR, which were designed to break the interaction between α-CT and the FnIII-1 domain. The D496A, R498E, D707A (the disease-causing mutation), and K703A mutants all showed greatly reduced activation (Figure 2B, and 2C).
evidence: This is an experimental result from cellular assays.

claim: Binding of insulin 1 to IR site 1 involves a tripartite interface: insulin–L1/α-CT (site 1a), insulin–FnIII-1 loop (site 1b), and α-CT–FnIII-1 loop (site 1b).
source: Taken together, binding of insulin 1 to IR site 1 involves a tripartite interface: insulin–L1/α-CT (site 1a), insulin–FnIII-1 loop (site 1b), and α-CT–FnIII-1 loop (site 1b).
evidence: This is a summary of the structural observations.

claim: Insulin 1 simultaneously engages site 1a and 1b to bridge the two IR protomers.
source: Thus, insulin 1 simultaneously engages site 1a and 1b to bridge the two IR protomers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: The strong tripartite interaction is critical for the formation of the 'T'-shaped active IR dimer by driving the rearrangement of the two IR protomers.
source: We propose that this strong tripartite interaction is critical for the formation of the 'T'-shaped active IR dimer by driving the rearrangement of the two IR protomers.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on structural and functional data.

claim: The binding mode of insulin 1 is reminiscent of the 'crosslinking' model proposed previously, except that this insulin crosslinks two sub-sites of site 1, as opposed to sites 1 and 2.
source: Conceptually, the binding mode of insulin 1 is reminiscent of the 'crosslinking' model proposed previously, except that this insulin crosslinks two sub-sites of site 1, as opposed to sites 1 and 2.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with prior models.

claim: A novel insulin-binding site for insulin 2 is located on the back side of a major β sheet of the FnIII-1 domain.
source: We have identified a novel insulin-binding site for insulin 2 binding, which is located on the back side of a major β sheet of the FnIII-1 domain (Figure 3A, and 3C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Residues from both A and B chains of insulin 2 contribute to the interaction at site 2.
source: Residues from both A and B chains of insulin 2 contribute to this interaction (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The residues involved in site 2 binding are located on the side of insulin opposite to that involved in the binding to site 1, and largely overlap with those in the insulin hexamer interface.
source: These residues are located on the side of insulin opposite to that involved in the binding to site 1, and largely overlap with those in the insulin hexamer interface (Table 2) (Weiss, 2009).
evidence: This is a structural comparison with prior knowledge.

claim: Several basic residues from IR FnIII-1, including Arg479, Lys484, Arg488, and Arg554, participate in the site 2 interaction.
source: Several basic residues from IR FnIII-1, including Arg479, Lys484, Arg488, and Arg554, participate in this interaction (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Hydrophobic residues from IR FnIII-1, such as Leu486, Leu552, and Pro537, pack tightly against residues Leu A13, Tyr A14, Leu A16, Leu B6, Ala B14, Leu B17, and Val B18 in insulin.
source: In addition, hydrophobic residues from IR FnIII-1, such as Leu486, Leu552, and Pro537, pack tightly against residues Leu A13, Tyr A14, Leu A16, Leu B6, Ala B14, Leu B17, and Val B18 in insulin (Figure 3B, and Table 2).
evidence: This is a detailed structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Many site 2 residues are conserved in vertebrate IR proteins, but some are not conserved in the IGF1R.
source: Many site 2 residues are conserved in vertebrate IR proteins, but some are not conserved in the IGF1R (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from sequence alignment analysis.

claim: There are no major structural differences between the free and receptor-bound insulin.
source: We superimposed the model of receptor-bound insulin 2 onto that of free insulin, which was previously determined by X-ray crystallography (PDB: 1MSO) (Smith et al., 2003). This comparison revealed no major structural differences between the free and bound insulin.
evidence: This is a result from structural comparison.

claim: Most of the insulin residues involved in the binding to site 2 have been correctly mapped by alanine scanning mutagenesis in previous work.
source: Most of the insulin residues involved in the binding to site 2, which include Ile A10, Ser A12, Leu A13, Glu A17, His B10, Glu B13, and Leu B17, have been correctly mapped by alanine scanning mutagenesis in the previous work (De Meyts, 2015; Kristensen et al., 1997), and these insulin site 2 mutations markedly reduced receptor-binding affinity (De Meyts, 2015; Kristensen et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a comparison of current structural findings with prior mutagenesis data.

claim: Most of the previously defined site 2 residues of insulin do not contact IR at site 1b.
source: Importantly, most of these previously defined site 2 residues of insulin do not contact IR at site 1b.
evidence: This is a structural comparison.

claim: The previous study incorrectly assigned site 1b as site 2.
source: Thus, the previous study (Scapin et al., 2018) has incorrectly assigned site 1b as site 2.
evidence: This is a correction of prior work based on current structural findings.

claim: The structure of the IR–insulin complex represents the first structure of the fully liganded, active IR.
source: Our structure of the IR–insulin complex has revealed the authentic site 2 of IR–insulin binding and represents the first structure of the fully liganded, active IR.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current structure.

claim: All IR mutants at site 2 (Y477A, R479E, K484E, R488E, P536A, P537A, L552A, and R554E) showed decreased insulin-dependent activation.
source: Next, we introduced multiple mutations in IR (Y477A, R479E, K484E, R488E, P536A, P537A, L552A, and R554E) designed to weaken this insulin 2-binding interface. Consistent with our structure-based predictions, all these IR mutants showed decreased insulin-dependent activation (Figure 3D, and 3E).
evidence: This is an experimental result from cellular assays.

claim: The K484E and L552A mutants were the most defective among the site 2 mutants.
source: Among them, the K484E and L552A mutants were the most defective.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from cellular assays.

claim: The IR K484E/L552A double mutant (site 2 mutant) was defective in insulin-dependent activation in a wide range of insulin concentrations.
source: In a dose-response assay, the IR K484E/L552A double mutant (site 2 mutant) was defective in insulin-dependent activation in a wide range of insulin concentrations (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), although the effect of this site 2 mutation was not as severe as that of the site 1 R14E mutation.
evidence: This is an experimental result from dose-response assays.

claim: The IR site 2 K484E/L552A mutant exhibited much weaker insulin-binding affinity compared to wild-type IR, particularly at physiological concentrations of insulin.
source: Furthermore, both cell-based and in vitro insulin-binding assays showed that the IR site 2 K484E/L552A mutant indeed exhibited much weaker insulin-binding affinity, as compared to wild-type IR, particularly at the physiological concentrations of insulin (Figure 3G and H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is an experimental result from binding assays.

claim: All site 2 IR mutants can localize to the plasma membrane, similar to wild-type IR.
source: Moreover, all site 2 IR mutants can localize to the plasma membrane, similar to wild-type IR (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the introduced mutations are unlikely to induce protein mis-localization or misfolding.
evidence: This is an experimental result from immunofluorescence microscopy.

claim: The results validate the importance of insulin 2 binding to site 2 of IR in insulin-dependent activation of IR.
source: These results validate the importance of insulin 2 binding to site 2 of IR in insulin-dependent activation of IR.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutagenesis and functional assays.

claim: The structures of the L1/CR segment and the FnIII-1/-2/-3 segment of insulin-bound IR can be superimposed perfectly onto those of apo-IR.
source: The structures of the L1/CR segment and the FnIII-1/-2/-3 segment of insulin-bound IR can be superimposed perfectly onto those of apo-IR, suggesting that no domain rotations occur in these two structural segments during insulin binding.
evidence: This is a result from structural comparison.

claim: No domain rotations occur in the L1/CR segment and the FnIII-1/-2/-3 segment during insulin binding.
source: The structures of the L1/CR segment and the FnIII-1/-2/-3 segment of insulin-bound IR can be superimposed perfectly onto those of apo-IR, suggesting that no domain rotations occur in these two structural segments during insulin binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claim: The overall structure of the IR protomer with insulin bound is more compacted, as a result of two large hinge motions around the L2 domain.
source: However, the overall structure of the IR protomer with insulin bound is more compacted, as a result of two large hinge motions around the L2 domain (Figure 4A, B and C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparison of apo and insulin-bound forms.

claim: A large conformational change takes place between the CR and L2 domains, with the loop connecting CR and L2 (residues 302–310) as the hinge.
source: A large conformational change takes place between the CR and L2 domains, with the loop connecting CR and L2 (residues 302–310) as the hinge (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The hinge loop (residues 302–310) has different conformations in apo- and insulin-bound IR.
source: This hinge loop has different conformations in apo- and insulin-bound IR (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparison of apo and insulin-bound forms.

claim: Glu287 and Lys310 form a salt bridge to stabilize the insulin-bound loop conformation.
source: In particular, Glu287 and Lys310 form a salt bridge to stabilize the insulin-bound loop conformation.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The L1/CR domains of IR rotate ~90° toward the L2 domain upon insulin binding.
source: Along with the conformational change of the hinge loop, the L1/CR domains of IR rotate ~90° toward the L2 domain upon insulin binding, creating two new inter-domain contacts (Figure 4B, and 4C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparison of apo and insulin-bound forms.

claim: The first new inter-domain contact is formed by Glu697 and Phe701 in the N-terminal portion of α-CT and Arg345 and Gly346 on the lateral surface of the β sheet in the L2 domain.
source: The first contact is formed by Glu697 and Phe701 in the N-terminal portion of α-CT and Arg345 and Gly346 on the lateral surface of the β sheet in the L2 domain (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: α-CT can simultaneously engage both L1 and L2 domains of the other IR protomer, tethering these two domains together.
source: As a result, α-CT can simultaneously engage both L1 and L2 domains of the other IR protomer, tethering these two domains together.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation.

claim: Another new contact is formed mainly through the interaction between a loop (residues 85–90) of the L1 domain and the first α-helix (residues 323–331) of the L2 domain.
source: Another new contact is formed mainly through the interaction between a loop (residues 85–90) of the L1 domain and the first α-helix (residues 323–331) of the L2 domain.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Another hinge motion upon insulin binding occurs around the linker between the L2 and FnIII-1 domains, resulting in a new inter-domain interaction between residues 454–460 of L2 and residues 572–578 in a loop of FnIII-1.
source: Another hinge motion upon insulin binding occurs around the linker between the L2 and FnIII-1 domains, resulting in a new inter-domain interaction between residues 454–460 of L2 and residues 572–578 in a loop of FnIII-1.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: FnIII-1,-2, and -3 domains as a rigid body rotate away from the L2 domain by ~50°.
source: Consequently, FnIII-1,-2, and -3 domains as a rigid body rotate away from the L2 domain by ~50° (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparison of apo and insulin-bound forms.

claim: Through the combination of two hinge motions, the overall architecture of the IR protomer is converted to an inverted 'J' shape.
source: Through the combination of these two hinge motions, the overall architecture of the IR protomer is converted an inverted 'J' shape (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Two 'J'-shaped protomers make the 'T' shaped active dimer.
source: Two such promoters make the 'T' shaped active dimer.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The α-CT domain plays a critical role in stabilizing the active conformation of the IR protomer.
source: The α-CT domain plays a critical role in stabilizing the active conformation of the IR protomer.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and functional data.

claim: Glu697 of α-CT forms a salt bridge with Arg345 in the L2 domain.
source: In particular, Glu697 of α-CT forms a salt bridge with Arg345 in the L2 domain (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Both Glu697 and Arg345 are far away from the bound insulins.
source: Both residues are far away from the bound insulins.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Mutations of Glu697 and Arg345 to alanine diminished IR activation by insulin.
source: Mutations of Glu697 and Arg345 to alanine diminished IR activation by insulin (Figure 4E, and 4F).
evidence: This is an experimental result from cellular assays.

claim: Mutation of Glu695 in α-CT that was not involved in inter-domain interactions had no effect on IR activation.
source: In contrast, mutation of a neighboring residue Glu695 in α-CT that was not involved in inter-domain interactions had no effect (Figure 4E, and 4F).
evidence: This is an experimental result from cellular assays, serving as a negative control.

claim: A homotypic interaction between the FnIII-2 domains of the two active IR protomers was identified.
source: Finally, we have identified a homotypic interaction between the FnIII-2 domains of the two active IR protomers.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The FnIII-2–FnIII-2 interaction is mediated by residues 647–653 in an extended loop.
source: The FnIII-2–FnIII-2 interaction is mediated by residues 647–653 in an extended loop (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The FnIII-2–FnIII-2 interaction is likely to be functionally important.
source: This interaction is likely to be functionally important, however, as mutation of Lys649, which is located in the center of this dimer interface, diminished IR activation, whereas mutation of Lys652, which is at the periphery of this interface, had no effect (Figure 2E, and 2F).
evidence: This is an inference based on mutagenesis results.

claim: Mutation of Lys649 diminished IR activation.
source: This interaction is likely to be functionally important, however, as mutation of Lys649, which is located in the center of this dimer interface, diminished IR activation, whereas mutation of Lys652, which is at the periphery of this interface, had no effect (Figure 2E, and 2F).
evidence: This is an experimental result from cellular assays.

claim: Mutation of Lys652 had no effect on IR activation.
source: This interaction is likely to be functionally important, however, as mutation of Lys649, which is located in the center of this dimer interface, diminished IR activation, whereas mutation of Lys652, which is at the periphery of this interface, had no effect (Figure 2E, and 2F).
evidence: This is an experimental result from cellular assays, serving as a control.

claim: Similar homotypic interactions between membrane-proximal domains have been found in other RTKs.
source: Similar homotypic interactions between membrane-proximal domains have been found in other RTKs (Yuzawa et al., 2007).
evidence: This is prior knowledge from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: Homotypic interactions between membrane-proximal domains are thought to precisely position the two stalk domains at the cell membrane and help to bring the two intracellular kinase domains into proximity for trans-autophosphorylation.
source: These interactions are thought to precisely position the two stalk domains at the cell membrane and help to bring the two intracellular kinase domains into proximity for trans-autophosphorylation.
evidence: This is a general mechanistic interpretation based on knowledge of RTK activation.

claim: Optimal IR activation requires the binding of multiple insulins to both sites 1 and 2.
source: Our mutagenesis results have shown that optimal IR activation requires the binding of multiple insulins to both sites 1 and 2 (Figure 3F and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on mutagenesis and functional assays.

claim: Binding of at least one insulin to the two site 2s is required for the formation of the 'T'-shaped dimer.
source: In addition, our 3D classification results further suggest that binding of at least one insulin to the two site 2 s is required for the formation of the 'T'-shaped dimer.
evidence: This is an inference based on 3D classification results.

claim: Formation of the active IR dimer is mainly driven by the tripartite interface formed by insulin 1, L1, α-CT, and FnIII-1 at site 1.
source: According to the cryo-EM structure, formation of the active IR dimer is mainly driven by the tripartite interface formed by insulin 1, L1, α-CT, and FnIII-1 at site 1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Insulin binding to site 1 of apo-IR or IGF-1R can release the autoinhibited conformation, which is an important step during IR or IGF-1R activation.
source: Previous studies have suggested that insulin binding to site 1 of apo-IR or IGF-1R can release the autoinhibited conformation, which is an important step during IR or IGF-1R activation (Kavran et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is prior knowledge from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Insulin 1 bound at site 1a sterically clashes with the linker between the FnIII-1 and FnIII-2 domains in apo-IR.
source: We superimposed the L1 domain of insulin-bound IR, along with insulin 1, onto that of apo-IR. Insulin 1 bound at site 1a sterically clashes with the linker between the FnIII-1 and FnIII-2 domains in apo-IR (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an observation from structural superposition.

claim: Insulin 1 binding at site 1a will disrupt the inter-apo-protomer interaction 1 between L1 and FnIII-2 domains, which is important in maintaining the autoinhibited IR dimer.
source: Thus, insulin 1 binding at site 1a will disrupt the inter-apo-protomer interaction 1 between L1 and FnIII-2 domains, which is important in maintaining the autoinhibited IR dimer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural clash observed.

claim: IGF1 binding to site 1a separates the L1 domain of one protomer from the FnIII-2 domain of the other protomer.
source: Interestingly, the crystal structure of IGF-1R with IGF1 bound (Xu et al., 2018) shows that IGF1 binding to site 1a separates the L1 domain of one protomer from the FnIII-2 domain of the other protomer.
evidence: This is prior structural knowledge from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: The inter-apo-protomer interaction 2 between the L2 and FnIII-1 domains still exists in IGF-1R with IGF bound at site 1a, due to the long flexible linker between the CR and L2 domains.
source: However, due to the long flexible linker between the CR and L2 domains, the inter-apo-protomer interaction 2 between the L2 and FnIII-1 domains on the top part of the inverted 'V'-shaped dimer still exists, even with IGF bound at site1a.
evidence: This is an observation from the IGF-1R structure.

claim: One IGF molecule cannot completely break the autoinhibited conformation of IGF-1R.
source: This result indicates that one IGF molecule cannot completely break the autoinhibited conformation of IGF-1R.
evidence: This is an inference based on the IGF-1R structure.

claim: One insulin molecule is likely to be insufficient to break the autoinhibited IR dimer.
source: By analogy, one insulin molecule is likely to be insufficient to break the autoinhibited IR dimer.
evidence: This is an inference by analogy to the IGF-1R case.

claim: Thr A8 and Ser A9 of insulin 2 bound at site 2 clashes with a β-turn motif in the L2 domain of the apo-IR dimer.
source: We next superimposed insulin 2 and the FnIII-1 domain of insulin-bound IR dimer onto that of apo-IR dimer. Thr A8 and Ser A9 of insulin 2 bound at site 2 clashes with a β-turn motif in the L2 domain of the apo-IR dimer.
evidence: This is an observation from structural superposition.

claim: Insulin binding to site 2 will destabilize the inter-apo-protomer interaction 2 between the L2 domain of one protomer and the FnIII-1 domain of the other.
source: Thus, insulin binding to site 2 will destabilize the inter-apo-protomer interaction 2 between the L2 domain of one protomer and the FnIII-1 domain of the other (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural clash observed.

claim: The two insulins bound to sites 1a and 2 in the apo-IR clash with each other.
source: Furthermore, the two insulins bound to sites 1a and 2 in the apo-IR clash with each other (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an observation from structural superposition.

claim: The additional steric clashes generated by the simultaneous binding of two insulins to sites 1a and 2 may further drive the two apo-IR protomers apart and completely destabilize the autoinhibited IR dimer.
source: These additional steric clashes, generated by the simultaneous binding of two insulins to sites 1a and 2, may further drive the two apo-IR protomers apart and completely destabilize the autoinhibited IR dimer (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation based on structural observations.

claim: The full activation of IR requires the binding of both insulins 1 and 2.
source: This could explain why the full activation of IR requires the binding of both insulins 1 and 2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and functional data.

claim: Once the autoinhibited IR dimer is disrupted by insulin binding, each insulin protomer is free to undergo two hinge motions, forming an inverted 'J'-shaped protomer.
source: Once the autoinhibited IR dimer is disrupted by insulin binding, each insulin protomer is free to undergo two hinge motions, forming an inverted 'J'-shaped protomer (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: It is unclear how the two 'J'-shaped protomers form the 'T'-shaped dimer.
source: Based on the current models, it is still unclear how the two 'J'-shaped protomers form the 'T'-shaped dimer.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a gap in understanding.

claim: The formation of the 'T'-shaped dimer has to involve coordinated structural rearrangements and inter-protomer rotations.
source: This process has to involve coordinated structural rearrangements and inter-protomer rotations.
evidence: This is a general inference about the process.

claim: The 'T'-shaped active dimer is predominantly stabilized by a tripartite interface between insulin 1, L1, α-CT, and FnIII-1 domains, without the involvement of insulin 2.
source: The 'T'-shaped active dimer is predominantly stabilized by a tripartite interface between insulin 1, L1, α-CT, and FnIII-1 domains, without the involvement of insulin 2.
evidence: This is a structural observation and interpretation.

claim: The membrane proximal regions from both protomers are brought together by a homotypic interaction between the two FnIII-2 domains.
source: Moreover, the membrane proximal regions from both protomers is brought together by a homotypic interaction between the two FnIII-2 domains.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Structural rearrangements promote the lateral TM-TM interaction, and enable trans-autophosphorylation between the two intracellular kinase domains.
source: Finally, these structural rearrangements promote the lateral TM-TM interaction, and enable trans-autophosphorylation between the two intracellular kinase domains (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: An endocytosis pathway, which involves the binding of MAD2-BUBR1 as well as the clathrin adaptor protein AP2 to the IR intracellular domain, triggers the internalization of the active IR dimer and stops insulin signaling at the plasma membrane.
source: An endocytosis pathway, which involves the binding of MAD2-BUBR1 as well as the clathrin adaptor protein AP2 to the IR intracellular domain, then triggers the internalization of the active IR dimer and stops insulin signaling at the plasma membrane (Choi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is prior knowledge from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: Binding of maximally four insulins to two distinct types of sites disrupts the autoinhibited IR dimer.
source: Our structural and functional analyses indicate that binding of maximally four insulins to two distinct types of sites disrupt the autoinhibited IR dimer.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the structural and functional data.

claim: The relaxed IR dimer with insulin bound undergoes structural rearrangements to form a 'T'-shaped active dimer, which is stabilized by a tripartite interaction between insulin 1, L1, α-CT, and FnIII-1 domains.
source: The relaxed IR dimer with insulin bound then undergo structural rearrangements to form a 'T'-shaped active dimer, which is stabilized by a tripartite interaction between insulin 1, L1, α-CT, and FnIII-1 domains.
evidence: This is a summary of the mechanistic model based on structural data.

claim: The binding mode strongly supports the previous insulin 'cross-linking' model.
source: This binding mode strongly supports the previous insulin 'cross-linking' model.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior models.

claim: The 'T'-shaped IR active dimer is further stabilized by the homotypic interaction between the two FnIII-2 domains from the two protomers.
source: Additionally, we observed that the 'T'-shaped IR active dimer is further stabilized the homotypic interaction between the two FnIII-2 domains from the two protomers.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The specific conformation of IR dimer facilitates the dimerization of the TM domain, thereby bringing the two kinase domains into close proximity for trans-autophosphorylation.
source: This specific conformation of IR dimer facilitates the dimerization of the TM domain, thereby bringing the two kinase domains into close proximity for trans-autophosphorylation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: The study provides key mechanistic insight into the initiation of insulin signaling.
source: Our study provides key mechanistic insight into the initiation of insulin signaling and paves the road for the eventual therapeutic intervention of diseases caused by insulin dysregulation.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: The binding of multiple insulins to IR occurs with negative cooperativity.
source: De Meyts et al. (1973) have proposed that the binding of multiple insulins to IR occurs with negative cooperativity.
evidence: This is prior knowledge from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: Both dose-response curves of IR WT and site 2 mutant could be fitted with the Hill equation, with Hill coefficients of ~0.64 and ~0.42, respectively, which are indicative of negative cooperativity in insulin binding to IR.
source: To understand the cooperativity between the binding of multiple insulins to different sites, we obtained a dose-response curve of insulin-dependent activation of IR WT and the site 2 mutant (Figure 3F). Both dose-response curves of IR WT and site 2 mutant could be fitted with the Hill equation, with Hill coefficients of ~0.64 and~0.42, respectively, which are indicative of negative cooperativity in insulin binding to IR.
evidence: This is an experimental result from dose-response assays.

claim: The IR site 2 mutant exhibits even stronger negative cooperativity than wild-type IR.
source: Because the IR site 2 mutant exhibits even stronger negative cooperativity and because insulin binding to site 2 is required for maximum insulin binding and full activation of IR, our results suggest that insulin binding to site 2 might dampen the anti-cooperativity between insulin binding to site 1 and site 1'.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Hill coefficient measurements.

claim: Insulin binding to site 2 might dampen the anti-cooperativity between insulin binding to site 1 and site 1'.
source: Because the IR site 2 mutant exhibits even stronger negative cooperativity and because insulin binding to site 2 is required for maximum insulin binding and full activation of IR, our results suggest that insulin binding to site 2 might dampen the anti-cooperativity between insulin binding to site 1 and site 1'.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the cooperativity data.

claim: The combination of cooperative binding between sites 1 and 2 and anti-cooperativity binding between sites 1 and 1' likely underlies the complicated shapes of the binding curves between IR and insulin.
source: The combination of cooperative binding between sites 1 and 2 and anti-cooperativity binding between sites 1 and 1' likely underlies the complicated shapes of the binding curves between IR and insulin.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the binding data.

claim: This unique system allows IR to respond differently to a wide range of insulin concentrations that various tissues experience at different metabolic states.
source: This unique system allows IR to respond differently to a wide range of insulin concentrations that various tissues experience at different metabolic states (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the binding properties.

claim: Site 1 and site 2 are both required for optimal IR activation.
source: Our functional analyses indicate that site 1 and site 2 are both required for optimal IR activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on mutagenesis and functional assays.

claim: It remains unknown which site is occupied first.
source: It remains unknown which site is occupied first.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a gap in understanding.

claim: One insulin binding to site 1 happens first, but may only lead to a partially active IR with an asymmetrical conformation.
source: Based on the different binding affinities between these two sites and all the existing structural models, we speculate that one insulin binding to site 1 happens first, but may only lead to a partially active IR with an asymmetrical conformation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on binding affinity and structural data.

claim: The subsequent binding of one insulin to site 2 facilitates the binding of the second insulin 1 to site 1', and thereby drives the formation of the symmetrical dimer and full IR activation.
source: The subsequent binding of one insulin to site 2 facilitates the binding of the second insulin 1 to site 1', and thereby driving the formation of the symmetrical dimer and full IR activation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the activation mechanism.

claim: The hypothesis that binding of two site-1 insulins and at least one site-2 insulin is necessary to promote the formation of the 'T'-shaped IR dimer is partially supported by the structural model.
source: This hypothesis is partially supported by our new structural model that binding of two site-1 insulins and at least one site-2 insulin is necessary to promote the formation of the 'T'-shaped IR dimer.
evidence: This is a statement about the support for the hypothesis from structural data.

claim: Solving the structures of IR site 1 and 2 mutants is needed to further test the hypothesis about the order of insulin binding.
source: Solving the structures of IR site 1 and 2 mutants is needed to further test this hypothesis.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experiments.

claim: It is not known for certain how many insulins are required for IR activation.
source: We also do not know for certain how many insulins are required for IR activation.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty.

claim: At low insulin concentrations, IR with partial insulin occupancy (e.g. one insulin at site 1) can achieve asymmetric conformations and exhibit different levels of activation.
source: It is possible that, at low insulin concentrations, IR with partial insulin occupancy (e.g. one insulin at site 1) can achieve asymmetric conformations and exhibit different levels of activation (Weis et al., 2018) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a speculative possibility based on prior work.

claim: Insulin can trigger both the metabolic and mitogenic responses through IR.
source: In addition, insulin can trigger both the metabolic and mitogenic responses through IR (De Meyts, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The conformational differences of IR caused by different stoichiometries of bound insulins may provide a mechanism in defining insulin signaling specificity.
source: It is tempting to speculate that the conformational differences of IR caused by different stoichiometries of bound insulins may provide a mechanism in defining insulin signaling specificity, which could potentially allow the same ligand (i.e. insulin) to generate distinct signaling outputs from the same receptor (i.e. IR).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about signaling specificity.

claim: Future biophysical and in vivo experiments, preferably those involving single-molecule techniques, are required to define the intermediate steps of IR activation.
source: Future biophysical and in vivo experiments, preferably those involving single-molecule techniques, are required to define the intermediate steps of IR activation.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research directions.

claim: The structure of the fully liganded IR-insulin complex serves as an important guide for designing future experiments.
source: Our structure of the fully liganded IR-insulin complex serves as an important guide for designing these experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the current structure.
